attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his newsletter. He is not quoting the investor friend here.

semantics.note: The 'appears to' wording keeps the 'does seem to' hedge. It drops 'many of which are losing money', but that omission does not change the core claim. This is a tentative impression, not a firm assertion.

contract.note: The contract scores a plain reading even though the speaker hedged. Policy reserves plain-reading scoring for firm language. 'Does seem to' only reports how the program looks, which is graded confidence, so the claim should not be scored.

evidence.note: The executive order asks for computing resources and partnerships to be identified. It names no chip purchases, vendors or amounts, and that silence settles nothing either way.
This October DOE–NVIDIA–Oracle deal predates Genesis. It describes shared investment and access, not federal chip purchases from many vendors.
Contemporary reporting mentions industry interest and plans to build more supercomputers, with funding unclear. It shows no purchase commitments.

reviews.rationale: Marcus hedged with 'does seem to', so he reported a tentative impression rather than asserting that the government was buying chips. Hedged language is not scored. Even if it were, the packet shows no federal chip purchases from many vendors by November 27, and no record rules them out, so the result would be unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description of Sacks's posts. Sacks's words are the subject matter, not the claim.

semantics.note: The proposition captures the claimed reversal and the timing. Marcus's bracketed '[let this all crash]' is his own paraphrase. Sacks actually wrote 'can't afford to go backwards', about AI investment.

contract.note: Reading 'turnaround' as a change of position on bailouts is ordinary in a post about bailouts. Requiring timestamps for 'just hours before' is reasonable. The result depends on how 'turnaround' is read.

evidence.note: The original November 6 post rejects a federal AI bailout. This confirms the first part of the claim.
Confirms the November 24 post, displayed at 5:34 PM with no time zone. Its wording is about the risk of an investment reversal and does not endorse a bailout.
Next-day clarification in which Sacks says he still opposes a bailout. This cuts against the 'turnaround' reading, but it is Sacks describing his own position and comes after the November 24 post.
DOE launched Genesis on November 24, the same day as the post. The page gives no time, so 'hours before' cannot be checked.

reviews.rationale: Both Sacks posts exist with the dates Marcus gives, and Genesis launched on November 24. Whether the second post was a turnaround on bailouts is disputed: its text is about investment, and Sacks denied it the next day, yet the record does not settle the change of position either way. No timestamps establish the 'just hours before' timing. The key parts remain unsettled.
